paras: The attempted lynching of Joseph Sampson was an attempt by Black residents of Georgetown to lynch Sampson, described as "a white boy", on or about 18 April 1882, after he was said to have stabbed and killed a Black man named Wilson. The attempt failed when Sampson's friends took him away.

According to a two-sentence paragraph in the Pickens Sentinel, Sampson "stabbed and killed a colored rough named Wilson at Georgetown on Tuesday," which places the killing on 18 April. The paragraph gives no cause for the stabbing and does not say where in town it happened. It then states that "the negroes attempted to lynch young Sampson whose friends took him away," without describing how the attempt was made or how many took part.
No report of an arrest, inquest into Wilson's death, or charge against Sampson or the would-be lynchers appears in the coverage found.

The Pickens Sentinel, published at Pickens, South Carolina, printed the item on 20 April 1882 on its second page, without a headline or a credit line, beside an unrelated paragraph credited to the Augusta Chronicle. The paragraph identified both men by race, called Wilson a "rough", and stated Sampson's killing of him as fact rather than as a charge. It did not name the state, and no other paper carrying the story was found.
